context_blurb:
Washing your hands before a meal rests on one idea: microbes, living things too small to see, cause many diseases. Between the 1840s and the 1880s, four doctors and a chemist proved it, one fair test at a time, against doubters with real reasons.

Most doctors then blamed disease on miasma, bad air from rot, and not foolishly: filth and sickness did go together. Many believed in spontaneous generation, life arising from lifeless matter. A fair test uses a control group, kept like the test group but for the one thing tested.

In Vienna, Ignaz Semmelweis worked in a hospital with two birth clinics: doctors and students ran the First, midwives the Second. Childbed fever killed mothers in the First more than twice as often. The clinics took patients by turns, a day each. Since nobody chose, neither clinic could have been sent the sicker women: by accident, a controlled trial.

In March 1847 Semmelweis's friend Jakob Kolletschka died after a student's scalpel pricked him during an autopsy, his body damaged like the dead mothers'. Semmelweis reasoned that matter from the corpse had entered through the cut, only its way in, and could cause the fever. Doctors came to the mothers straight from autopsies; midwives did none.

From May, Semmelweis had the doctors scrub their hands in chlorinated lime, and his clinic's deaths fell from over eighteen in a hundred to about one by July. His chief, Johann Klein, wanted more than counts. Semmelweis could not say what his matter was or how it did harm, because no one could yet see it. Shunned by many doctors, he died in an asylum in 1865, before germ theory explained his washing.

In London, John Snow held that cholera, which starts in the gut, is swallowed in water. In 1854 he mapped Soho's deaths around the Broad Street pump, then sought a test that could sink his idea. Had bad air been the cause, the seventy-odd brewery men by the pump, who drank only beer, would have died as often as their neighbours. None fell seriously ill; they never drank its water.

The parish took the pump's handle off on 8 September; many tellings call that the proof, but Snow did not. Fatal cases had already been falling for days before the handle came off, from 143 on the first of the month to 12 that day, partly because people had fled. A step taken while deaths are already dropping cannot show it stopped them.

In Paris, the chemist Louis Pasteur faced Félix Pouchet, spontaneous generation's defender, who held that life needs air's oxygen to arise, so sealed broth proved nothing. Pasteur stretched a flask's neck into a long, open S, like a swan's, and boiled broth in it. Air passed freely through the open tip, so the broth had the oxygen Pouchet demanded, but dust and its microbes settled on the moist glass of the bend. It stayed clear for months.

Pouchet also said the long boil had ruined the broth as food for life. Pasteur snapped one neck off short, letting dust fall straight in, and the broth soon teemed. The boil, then, had not spoiled the broth as food for microbes.

In Glasgow, the surgeon Joseph Lister watched operation wounds rot, a rot blamed on air's oxygen, and lost close to half his amputees. If the rot came instead from Pasteur's living specks in the air, Lister could leave the air alone and kill the specks where they reached each wound. Using carbolic acid from 1865, he cut amputation deaths by two thirds, though critics wanted wards with and without it compared.

The country doctor Robert Koch set out to prove that rod-shaped microbes caused anthrax. He put matter from the spleens of anthrax-killed animals into tiny cuts in mice, and all died; mice given healthy spleen blood alongside them lived. Both groups got the same cut, so the killer was not the cut but something in the sick animals' matter. The comparison could not single out the rods, so Koch grew them alone for generations in fluid from an ox's eye, and they still caused anthrax.

The first of four steps named after him demands a germ in every sick body and no healthy one. Koch found cholera's comma-shaped germ in every victim he examined, then in healthy carriers too. Koch kept the germ as the cause and judged the first step too strict: a germ can live in people without making them ill.
